note:
v1, EXTREME AND MEAN: THE SEVENTH SONG, A SKELETON (Harry, 17 Nov about 03:40: "open up 2 new song slots"). The record's slow song: 80, where the other six run 100 to 138.
The riff is two cells, a long (three sixteenths) and a short (two), and one rule: every long becomes a long and a short, every short becomes a long. Apply it again and again and you get a pattern of longs and shorts that never falls into a loop, yet every stretch of it comes back, and it is the same at every size. So the band plays the one pattern at many sizes at once: the guitars' muted strokes are the smallest cells; where a cell of eight or five sixteenths begins the string is let ring; where one of thirteen or eight begins there is a chord; where one of thirty-four or twenty-one begins, a crash; and the song's own eight sections go long, short, long, long, short, long, short, long: the long ones heavy, the short ones quiet. The form is the riff, 78 times slower. The kit keeps common time against all of it and starts its count again with each section.
In the quiet sections a wire harp (new on this record) has no written notes: the engine is given the same rule and plays it, each short cell a step higher than the long one that made it. In the last section the harp plays over the band.
The title is Euclid's phrase for a line cut so that the whole is to the longer part as the longer is to the shorter. Such a cut has no common measure; neither has this riff.
WHERE THINGS ARE: heavy 0:00, quiet 0:44, heavy 1:11, heavy on A flat with four guitars 1:54, quiet 2:38, heavy 3:05, quiet 3:49, heavy with the harp 4:16, one chord 4:59.

v2, THE SAME TUNE AT EVERY SIZE (a whole-song round, taken openly: the draw was Odd Sympathy, which I passed; v1's note said the three quiet sections were the same nine bars three times).
The song's idea is one pattern at every size, and the band already plays it so in the heavy sections. Now the harps do too. The first quiet section is as it was: one harp, the tune on the smallest cells (three and two sixteenths). In the second there are two harps: the new one plays THE SAME TUNE on the next size of cell (five and three sixteenths), an octave lower. In the third there are three: the third plays it on cells of eight and five, an octave lower again. It is a canon in which nobody starts late: the voices start together and go at different speeds, and the speeds stand to each other as the long cell to the short. Because the larger cells are made of the smaller, every note of a slower harp falls exactly with a note of the faster ones.
The engine plays all of it from the one rule; no harp has a written note.

v3, BREATH FOR THE LARGEST SIZE (a palette round, as drawn: the part the song lacked, on a sound no other song has).
The band plays the one pattern at many sizes, but one size had no voice of its own: cells of 21 and 13 sixteenths, about four seconds and two and a half. That is as long as a note can usefully be held, so it is where a tune can be sung slowly. In the three four-guitar sections (1:54, 3:05, 4:16) a brass section, horns and trombones, now plays the harp's tune on those cells, one long note to a cell. Strings are plucked for the small sizes; breath holds the large one. It is the same tune again (the canon of v2 went down three sizes in the quiet sections; this is a fourth, in the heavy ones).
The brass is the engine's physical model of lips on a tube, the first wind instrument on the record.

When all four guitars pick the small riff again at 3:32, the kick goes the other way. Run the rule backwards once: a long of three sixteenths is a long of two and a short of one, a short of two is one long. So the foot stops doubling 'stroke, stroke, rest' and plays 'stroke, rest, stroke'; under each held chord it adds a pickup. After 21 sixteenths (3:36) the bass and the two inside guitars go with it: in each muted long cell the wall pair strikes twice and the low end answers in the gap. note: v13, FOUR KETTLEDRUMS (palette: the kick's soft strokes in the middle quiet section go to tuned drums; a new song-local patch, `em-kettle`, the record's first use of the engine's kettledrum modes). LISTEN FOR 2:38–3:05, and the last second and a half before the band at 3:05. One size of cell had no tune anywhere: 13 and 8 sixteenths. Under the band those cells are the chord; in the quiet sections they were only the foot, thirteen soft kicks. In the middle quiet section those thirteen strokes are now four kettledrums playing the harp's tune at that size, an octave under the lower harp: A♭, then C♭ and E♭, and on the last cell the one G♭. That last note is rolled, and while it rolls the pedal lets the head down a semitone, so the roll arrives on F with the band: the clean E and B go up to F and C there (v10), and the drum comes down to meet them. The first and third quiet sections keep their foot. WHAT I MEASURED: a stroke sings its written note (the kettle pulls the head's modes to 1 : 1.5 : 2); over the section the drums sit 3.6 dB under the two harps and level with the bowl, each stroke 1.8 to 4.6 dB under everything else together. The roll murmurs at the level of the rest, then for its last 0.4 s stands 5 to 6 dB over it; alone, its pitch holds G♭ until 0.56 s before the band and reads F on arrival. THE COST: the section is 0.46 LU louder (4.4 dB under the band before it; it was 4.9). Every other section, and all five excerpts on the three open cards, moved 0.03 dB or less (the file's loudness trim). Full renders 99.767 → 99.771 and 99.826 → 99.833 (seeds 0, 11), −10.1 LUFS. WHAT THE BENCH TAUGHT (in sounds.md): a roll's strokes must fall a whole, even number of the head's cycles apart or they cancel (strokes every 75 ms left a hole 14 dB deep); `bright` does nothing to a kettle; an expr_path runs to the release, so the patch needs gate=1. WHAT I CANNOT KNOW: whether soft kettledrums under two harps and a bowl sound like an orchestra pit or like a film score; whether the roll helps the return or crowds the guitar's swelling A♭. Not heard by me. note: SECTION w1, THE TWO LETTERS ON TWO SIDES. LISTEN FOR 0:00–0:10.3, the song’s first cell of 55 sixteenths (flagged static; the stretch the last two notes called unworked). The riff is a word in two letters, long and short, and until now both guitars said every stroke of it together. Here they spell it apart: the chords and the ringing strings are still both guitars, but between them the clipped strokes inside long cells are the left guitar’s alone and the ones inside short cells the right’s. Thirteen strokes left, eight right: the ratio in the title. Bass and foot stay in the middle on every stroke. At 0:10.3, on the first G♭ chord, the two play as one again, and the log drum (on the right) takes the short cells the right guitar has just been saying alone. By subtraction only: 21 strokes are each played by one guitar where two played them (gl gives up 8, gr 13); no note is added or moved, and nothing else in the song changes. MEASURED, mastered seed 0, per stroke: in the guitar bands the picture swings from centred to −6.2 dB left / +5.4 right at 250 Hz–1 kHz and −9.7 / +8.5 at 1–6 kHz (the least-separated stroke is still 4.4 dB to its side); below 250 Hz nothing moves (bass and kick, −0.1 dB). COST: those strokes carry 2.0–2.4 dB less guitar, and the ten seconds read 0.54 dB lower overall; the five chords are unchanged (0.00 dB), and the step up into the G♭ chord at 0:10.3 grows from +0.3 to +1.0 dB. From 0:10.3 on, the residual is −55.6 dB or lower; the five excerpts on the three cards and the kettledrums moved 0.02 dB (the master’s gain) and keep every note. Scores level, seeds 0/11: 99.771/99.833 → 99.778/99.839; seed 5 reads 99.867; −10.1 LUFS, −1.29 dBTP. Kept for the idea, not the hundredths. WHAT I CANNOT KNOW: whether a slow, heavy opening wants its chugs split left and right or whether that makes the first ten seconds lighter than the em-slow question can afford. note: PALETTE, THE BOW HOLDS THE ROOT: a section of double basses, bowed (the library's contrabass, the engine's physical bow; no other song on the record uses it; new track, five notes). LISTEN FOR 3:05–3:49, the return to F, and most of all the gaps between the strokes. Every size of cell but one had a voice of its own: strokes (3 and 2), the ringing string (8 and 5), kettledrums (13 and 8), a breath of brass (21 and 13), a crash (34 and 21). Cells of 55 and 34 are the root, and nothing ever held a root: it was only struck again. 55 sixteenths is 10.3 seconds, more than a breath and about what one slow bow can hold. So the basses draw one bow to a cell: F (3:05.1), G flat (3:15.4), F (3:21.8), F (3:32.1), G flat (3:42.4), an octave over the guitars' low string. Plucked for the small sizes, breath for the large, the bow for the one above. It is the first thing in a heavy section that sounds through the riff's rests, and it bears on the open question whether the slow song is heavy; that card's three excerpts are untouched. No other part changed. note:
v16, THE IRON SAYS FIVE AND THREE (palette: a new part on a new song-local patch, em-iron; no other song on the record has struck iron). LISTEN FOR 1:54.4–2:11.1, the first 89 sixteenths of the tutti in A flat, the stretch the last notes called unworked. In the heavy sections one size of cell had no voice: 5 and 3 sixteenths (the second harp has them in the quiet sections; under the band they were only a slightly harder stroke). Now a hammer on an iron bar strikes the head of every such cell, thirteen long and eight short, so for these seventeen seconds seven sizes sound at once: strokes, iron, the ringing string, the chord, the brass's breath, the crash and the root. The kit goes on counting four against it; 7 of the 21 strokes fall on a china quarter and 14 between. The iron stops where the walls take up the bowl's chords at 2:11.1. No stroke of the band is added, moved or removed: each iron stroke is on one the kick already plays.
THE BAR: its overtones are cut in extreme and mean ratio. Each partial is to the next as the long cell to the short (1 : 1.618 : 2.618 : 4.236 : 6.854 ...), so each partial's frequency is the sum of the two below it: the rule the riff is made by, in the sound. Two bars: a long cell is struck on the bar tuned to the ground (A flat, then A from 2:04.7), a short cell on a bar a golden cut shorter, 833 cents up, between a minor and a major sixth. Every partial of the short bar is a partial of the long one: the short bar is the long bar without its lowest note. So the ear gets the word itself as two pitches: low high low low high low high low low high ...
WHAT I MEASURED: the bar alone sounds 415.3, 672.0, 1087.3, 1759.3, 2846.6, 4605.8 and 7452.4 Hz on A flat (each the sum of the two before; the fourth is the A the ground rises to), the short bar 672.0 upwards; a stroke falls 8 dB in 200 ms and 18 to 19 in 400. FIRST BENCH, not kept: at -9 dB the iron stood 5.8 dB under the band (K) and, on the long bar's strokes, 8 dB OVER it at 600–1200 Hz (4 on the short bar's), a soloist. Kept at -15 dB, raw seed 0: 11.8 dB under the band; in a stroke's first 60 ms the long bar is 2.4 dB over the band at 600–1200 Hz and the short bar 1.7 under there and 2.5 under at 2.5–5 kHz; the stretch gains 0.7 dB at 500–2000 Hz, 0.2 at 250–500 (where chirper-one's read has this section 3.8 over the records) and 0.3 or less above 2 kHz, +0.28 LU. Finished, the master holds the level: the stretch reads -8.77 -> -8.75 LUFS (seed 0; 0.02 or less on seeds 11 and 5), and a long-bar stroke still adds 1.3 dB over v15 at 600–1200 Hz. Every other stretch, the five excerpts on the three cards among them, is within 0.01 LU and -70.6 dB or lower gain-matched (the file's trim moved 0.004 dB or less).
SCORE, seeds 0/11/5: 99.896/99.933/99.953 -> 99.894/99.930/99.951 (the spectrum term, 0.02–0.03). Level; kept on judgment, unheard, for the part. -10.1 LUFS, -1.29 dBTP. C10T7_IRON='' regenerates v15 byte for byte; ARCO and SIDES empty still give v14 and v13.
WHAT I CANNOT KNOW: whether hammered iron over four guitars is weight or a novelty; whether two inharmonic bars a golden sixth apart sound like one instrument or like one bar out of tune with the brass (its first note, A flat 4, is the long bar's pitch); whether five-and-three is heard against the china's four or only as clatter. Not checked by ear. v15 then v16, 1:51.4–2:13.0: http://pocket4:8790/clips/three-c10-t7-v16-iron-five-and-three-ab.mp3 ; the iron with only the kit, 1:53.9–2:12.3 (level raised, for inspection): http://pocket4:8790/clips/three-c10-t7-v16-iron-five-and-three-kit.mp3 . note:
v17, SECTION w5 (1:36–2:00), ONE STROKE AND A REST, AT THE SIZE OF THE ROOT. LISTEN FOR 1:51.9–1:54.4, the last 2.4 seconds before the tutti in A flat. Everywhere else in the song a quiet section stands between two heavy ones; between the third section and the fourth (the form is L S L L S L S L) there was nothing: the riff ran straight into the tutti behind eight sixteenths of tom fill that the guitars played through. The rule says what belongs there. A short cell is one stroke and a rest; the third section's last cell of 34 is a short one, and 34 is 21 and 13. So the band plays its 21 and RESTS its 13: at 1:51.9 the two guitars, the bass and the foot stop, the largest rest in the song (the smallest is one sixteenth). The kit is not in the pattern and does not stop: its china goes on counting quarters through the hole. In the hole the steel's last bend, A flat falling to F, is heard alone for a second (1:51.9–1:52.9). Then the drummer, who has kept four against the pattern all song, says it: the toms play exactly the five strokes the guitars leave out (two, the ringing one, two: 1:52.9, 1:53.1, 1:53.4, 1:53.8, 1:54.0), one sixteenth of china, and the tutti lands at 1:54.4. The other four heavy sections keep their old fill. By subtraction: guitars, bass and kick each lose seven strokes; the old fill's six toms and two snares become five toms; the steel, the china and every other part are as they were.
WHAT I MEASURED: raw, seed 0, the band is 40 dB down within 100 ms of the stop and 80 down by 0.4 s (a hard stop, no tail); in the hole the steel alone and the cymbals alone are level (-30.1 and -30.8 K), together 5.6 dB under the band that was there; the toms' stretch is 4.1 under. The step up into the tutti (the second before against the second after) goes from 1.2 to 5.4 dB raw and from 0.6 to 3.0 dB finished (seeds 11 and 5: 0.7 -> 3.2, 0.8 -> 2.8; the limiter had been holding the band down). Nothing differs before the stop (to 1.6 ms). The tutti's first 3.6 seconds read -10 to -12 dB against v16 (the last tom ringing into it, and the bass and guitars starting from rest) at the same level (within 0.05 LU); from 1:58 on it is untouched.
THE FILE: a hole of 2.4 seconds made the file measure 0.028 dB quieter, so every other bar came out that much louder; the loudness target is now -10.028 and they are back (0.007 dB or less, all seeds). Every other stretch, the five excerpts on the three cards among them, is within 0.01 LU and -65.8 dB or lower gain-matched.
SCORE, seeds 0/11/5: 99.894/99.930/99.951 -> 99.874/99.911/99.933 (the spectrum term, 0.16–0.18: 2.4 seconds without the band's low end). Level; kept on judgment, unheard, for the break. -10.1 LUFS, -1.29 dBTP. C10T7_REST='' regenerates v16 byte for byte; IRON and ARCO empty still give v15 and v14.
WHAT I CANNOT KNOW: whether 2.4 seconds without the band is a held breath or a hole in a slow song that is already asked whether it is heavy or only slow; whether the steel alone (it was written to sit over guitars) is a voice or a leftover; whether five tom strokes in the riff's rhythm read as the riff or as a fill that stumbles.
